reader.targetFrench: Je suis dans un café avec ma femme, mon fils et ma belle-mère.
reader.supportEnglish: I am in a café with my wife, my son, and my mother-in-law.

reader.targetFrench: Je dis d'abord au serveur : « Je veux commander pour tout le monde, s'il vous plaît. »
reader.supportEnglish: First, I say to the waiter: I want to order for everyone, please.

reader.targetFrench: Pour moi, un café au lait et des œufs brouillés.
reader.supportEnglish: For me, a coffee with milk and some scrambled eggs.

reader.targetFrench: Pour ma femme, un thé et un sandwich au jambon, sans fromage.
reader.supportEnglish: For my wife, a tea and a ham sandwich, without cheese.

reader.targetFrench: Mon fils va prendre un jus d'orange et un petit pain sucré.
reader.supportEnglish: My son is going to have orange juice and a sweet roll.

reader.targetFrench: Ma belle-mère veut un café décaféiné et du pain grillé avec du beurre.
reader.supportEnglish: My mother-in-law wants a decaf coffee and toast with butter.

reader.targetFrench: Puis je répète la commande : « C'est correct ? Le thé est pour elle, c'est bien ça ? »
reader.supportEnglish: Then, I repeat the order: Is that correct? The tea is for her, right?

reader.targetFrench: Le serveur sourit et dit : « Tout est correct, je vous apporte ça tout de suite. »
reader.supportEnglish: The waiter smiles and says: Everything is right, I'll bring it right away.

reader.targetFrench: À la fin, je demande l'addition à la table.
reader.supportEnglish: At the end, I ask for the check at the table.

forms.exampleFrench: Je veux commander pour tout le monde.
forms.exampleEnglish: I want to order for everyone.
forms.explanationEnglish: Commander is the usual French verb for ordering food. Pedir has a stem change (e to i) in Spanish; French commander is a regular -er verb, so no stem change applies. For asking for the check, the source sentence 'pido la cuenta' is rendered with demander: 'je demande l'addition'.

forms.exampleFrench: Ma belle-mère veut un café décaféiné.
forms.exampleEnglish: My mother-in-law wants a decaf coffee.
forms.explanationEnglish: Vouloir is irregular (je veux, tu veux, il/elle veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils veulent). Here the third-person form veut means 'wants' literally, not a softened 'would like'. Querer's e-to-ie stem change in Spanish corresponds to the irregular French stem in veut.

forms.exampleFrench: Mon fils va prendre un jus d'orange.
forms.exampleEnglish: My son is going to have orange juice.
forms.explanationEnglish: Prendre covers 'have (a drink)' and 'take' in the source sense. 'Va prendre' uses aller plus an infinitive for the near future, matching 'va a tomar'. Prendre is irregular: je prends, il prend, nous prenons, ils prennent.

forms.exampleFrench: Je répète la commande pour confirmer.
forms.exampleEnglish: I repeat the order to confirm.
forms.explanationEnglish: Répéter is a regular -er verb with the accent on the é in the stem (je répète). Spanish repetir has an e-to-i stem change, which has no French counterpart here. Used for the confirmation step.

forms.exampleFrench: Je vous apporte ça tout de suite.
forms.explanationEnglish: Apporter is a regular -er verb meaning 'to bring'. The Spanish irregular yo form traigo has no French irregularity here: j'apporte. Vous is the polite form the waiter uses with the customer.

roles.englishDescription: You, ordering breakfast for a group of three people plus yourself, then confirming who gets what.
The server who takes the order, repeats it when asked, and brings the check at the end.

speaking.openingFrench: Bonjour ! Je veux commander pour tout le monde. Pour ma femme, un thé et un sandwich au jambon, sans fromage. C'est bien ça ?
objectivesEnglish: Open the order by saying you want to order for everyone.
Assign items to each person with pour moi and pour elle (or pour ma femme, pour mon fils, pour ma belle-mère).
Say 'without cheese' with sans for an exclusion.
Confirm who gets what by repeating the order before the server leaves.
Ask for the check at the end.

notes: Literal fidelity: 'I want' is rendered as 'Je veux' (not 'Je voudrais'), and 'wants' as 'veut' (not 'voudrait'). 'Je voudrais' is a softer, more polite form and is not used in this packet. The earlier French packet's 'Je voudrais' and 'Ma belle-mère voudrait' were changed for this reason. Flag for the reviewer: 'Je veux' may sound blunt in a real café; this is the literal source meaning.

'Mother-in-law' is rendered as 'belle-mère' (literal sense of the source). 'Family assignments' are rendered with pour moi, pour ma femme, pour mon fils, pour ma belle-mère, and pour elle, matching the source's assignment pattern.

'Sweet roll' is rendered as 'petit pain sucré', the closest equivalent of the source sense. A local French pastry (viennoiserie such as a croissant or pain au chocolat) is a different item and is not used. Uncertainty: the Spanish source notes pan dulce as a regional item, so the French equivalent is a judgment call.
'Ham sandwich' is rendered as 'sandwich au jambon'. 'Jambon-beurre' is a specific French sandwich and is not used, to avoid changing the item.
'Decaf' is rendered as 'décaféiné' (the full form). Flag: in everyday French, 'déca' is common informal speech; the full word is used for literal fidelity.
'Check' is rendered as 'l'addition' (not 'la note', which is used for a different sense in some regions). 'Check' appears both as a card (l'addition) and as a phrase (L'addition, s'il vous plaît.).

Pedir is rendered as 'commander' for ordering food and as 'demander' for asking for the check. Flag: the verb choice for 'ask for' is context-dependent and a reviewer may prefer one form consistently.
Tomar (to have a drink) is rendered as 'prendre', which covers 'have' and 'take'. 'Boire' would be too narrow for food.
Traer ('to bring') is rendered as 'apporter'. The waiter uses 'vous' (polite form), matching the source's usted register.

Waiter gender: the source notes 'mesera' for a woman. The French feminine is 'serveuse'. The card uses 'le serveur' (masculine) as the default, matching the source's 'mesero'. Flag for a reviewer if a feminine card is wanted.

'Is that correct?' is rendered as 'C'est correct ?' in the reader and 'La commande est-elle correcte ?' on the card. Both are literal. 'Tout est correct' is used for 'Everything is right' (literal 'correct'); a more idiomatic 'Tout est bien' is possible but changes the English meaning.
Stage-local IDs core:8:word:1 to core:8:word:18 and core:8:line:1 to core:8:line:9 are preserved, with 18 cards and 9 reader turns, in source order.
The French target text was authored from the English meanings; the Spanish source was used only for verb examples and item context. No audio is provided or implied.
